documents.title: GenAI Syllabus Statements
documents.summary: Provost-and-Senate guidance on GenAI syllabus statements. It sets a default that GenAI needs written instructor permission and is scholastic dishonesty otherwise, then gives instructors required elements and two sample statements (prohibited, permitted) to adapt.
documents.stance_why: The page opens "Instructors at the University may allow or prohibit the use of Generative AI (GenAI) tools in their courses", and offers a prohibited template and a permitted template; it hands the decision to instructors, so the stance is delegates with two tiers.

units.why: The passage says instructors "may allow or prohibit" GenAI in their courses, so the decision sits with each instructor, which is P04 (per-instructor rule), not a university-wide stance.
units.anchor: Instructors at the University may allow or prohibit the use of Generative AI (GenAI) tools

units.why: Instructors are "strongly encouraged to include a clear syllabus statement", which asks for an AI statement in the syllabus (P09); "strongly encouraged" makes it should rather than must.
units.anchor: strongly encouraged to include a clear syllabus statement outlining their expectations

units.why: This says what a course policy "should define", i.e. the content of the syllabus AI statement, so P09 fits better than P04 because it does not say who decides.
units.anchor: should define acceptable and unacceptable uses of GenAI, reference relevant academic policies
units.policy: A well-crafted course policy defines acceptable and unacceptable uses of GenAI, references relevant academic policies, and supports students in reaching compliance.

units.why: "Students should consult their instructors if they are unsure" is the ask-when-unsure rule (P10).
units.anchor: Students should consult their instructors if they are unsure what constitutes acceptable use

units.why: The page states it was "developed in collaboration with the Senate Committee on Educational Policy", which says by whom the guidance was made (P84).
units.anchor: developed in collaboration with the Senate Committee on Educational Policy

units.why: AI in coursework "requires written instructor permission", so it is off unless the instructor says yes. That is a default-when-silent rule (P06); P01 does not fit because the instructor can grant permission.
units.anchor: Use of generative artificial intelligence as part of coursework requires written instructor permission

units.why: Instructors are told to "Provide specific examples" of allowed and disallowed use, which is content of the syllabus statement (P09).
units.anchor: Provide specific examples of how students may or may not use GenAI tools

units.why: "you may limit AI to specific tasks or assignments" lets the rule vary per task or assignment (P04).
units.anchor: you may limit AI to specific tasks or assignments

units.why: Instructors should "Encourage students to consult and confirm the policy before starting", an ask-first rule (P10).
units.anchor: Encourage students to consult and confirm the policy before starting an assignment

units.why: Instructors must "Clearly state" whether licensed tools are allowed, even under a ban. This is a syllabus statement requirement (P09); P17 is for providing a tool, which this does not do.
units.anchor: Clearly state whether UMN-licensed Generative AI tools are permitted in the course
units.fit_note: Specifically requires a tool-by-tool statement, including when other GenAI use is prohibited.

units.why: "encouraged to recommend UMN-licensed tools" points instructors to institution-licensed tools (P92); it is not one course's own tool (P17).
units.anchor: Instructors are encouraged to recommend UMN-licensed tools

units.why: The licensed tools are "available to students at no cost", an equal-access fact (P51).
units.anchor: available to students at no cost through their UMN login
units.fit_note: States that licensed tools are free to students; does not say AI is optional or that alternatives exist.

units.why: Unlicensed tools "may not meet these standards" (accessibility and privacy), which supports preferring vetted tools (P50); students still "may choose" them independently.
units.anchor: Third-party tools that fall outside the University’s licensing agreements may not meet these standards
units.fit_note: Also says students may choose third-party tools on their own.

units.why: Faculty who want to buy a third-party AI tool "are encouraged to consult" the software purchase request process, a review step before deploying a tool (P65).

units.anchor: may not be used for course assignments except as explicitly authorized by an instructor

units.why: The Conduct Code quote defines cheating to include "unauthorized use of online learning support and testing platforms"; because GenAI is classed as such a platform, unauthorized use is scholastic dishonesty (P36).

units.why: Posting "faculty-provided course materials" on learning platforms is listed as scholastic dishonesty; since GenAI counts as such a platform, this bars uploading course materials to AI tools (P49).

units.why: The Administrative Policy "provides instructors the discretion to award a grade of an F or N" for scholastic dishonesty, a concrete penalty stated in advance (P37).

units.why: Instructors "should indicate any tools" used to uncover dishonesty, i.e. tell students about checking tools in the syllabus. P40 is the nearest type; it is about using such tools.

units.fit_note: Requires telling students in advance which detection tools may be used; does not itself authorize the tools.

units.anchor: input student work into GenAI tools without the student’s explicit written consent

units.anchor: policies, practices, and approved tools may be updated anytime during the semester as technology evolves

documents.title: Teaching with Generative AI
documents.summary: A Teaching Support resource hub that links instructors to syllabus statements, GenAI courses, tool guides, and campus and college resources. It does not set a stance for student AI use.
documents.stance_why: The page is a list of resources "on how to best incorporate generative AI into your teaching practices" and leaves any rule on student AI use to instructors, so it delegates.

units.why: The GenAI+U student course "equips UMN students with the knowledge, skills, and ethical understanding" to use AI responsibly, an AI-literacy offering for students (P70).
units.anchor: equips UMN students with the knowledge, skills, and ethical understanding necessary to effectively and responsibly

units.why: The instructor guide to AI literacy helps faculty understand AI "regardless of whether you plan to embrace these tools", support for faculty learning (P63).
units.anchor: guide for University of Minnesota instructors to navigate the transformative role of Generative AI in

units.why: The resource "outlines essential considerations for using GenAI for classroom assessment", advice on instructors using AI in teaching work (P59); it sets no condition, so P101 does not fit.
units.anchor: outlines essential considerations for using GenAI for classroom assessment
units.fit_note: Only lists questions to consider (motivation, efficacy, students' responses); gives no rule.

units.why: The integrity course for instructors "covers student engagement strategies, AI detection tools, citation practices, assignment design" and responding to misuse, training for faculty (P63).
units.anchor: covers student engagement strategies, AI detection tools, citation practices, assignment design, and steps for responding

units.why: Example syllabus statements "developed by the Senate Committee on Educational Policy" are offered as help for instructors writing course policy (P63).
units.anchor: developed by the Senate Committee on Educational Policy
units.fit_note: A pointer to example statements; no rule.

units.why: Galleries show "the spectrum of GenAI usage ... from AI-prohibitive to using AI to augment learning", examples to help instructors choose (P63) rather than a tier system (P05).
units.anchor: the spectrum of GenAI usage in (or not) in coursework (from AI-prohibitive to using AI
units.fit_note: Shows that practice spans a range; defines no tiers.

units.why: Instructors are directed to "leverage approved generative AI tools to support student learning", i.e. use the institution-approved tools (P92).
units.anchor: Learn how to leverage approved generative AI tools to support student learning

units.why: The page lists separate college, campus and graduate-school AI resources (LATIS, CEHD, UMD), showing that units have their own guidance (P85).
units.anchor: Campus or College Specific Teaching Resources
units.fit_note: Only links to unit-specific resources; does not say units may set different rules.

units.why: The Libraries video "introduces some of the ethical issues and other risks that AI tools like ChatGPT present", naming ethical concerns (P53).
units.anchor: introduces some of the ethical issues and other risks that AI tools like ChatGPT present
units.fit_note: Mentions ethical issues and risks without naming specific harms.

units.why: "Navigating AI @UMN" "brings together resources for faculty, staff, and students to responsibly leverage, and innovate with, AI", a community-wide AI guidance hub (P70).
units.anchor: brings together resources for faculty, staff, and students to responsibly leverage, and innovate with, AI
units.fit_note: A hub of resources rather than training.

units.why: Instructors "may wish to share" the GenAI+U student training with students, linking students to AI-literacy training (P70).
units.anchor: Instructors may wish to share this resource with their students

units.why: The AI community of practice is "Open to all" staff, faculty and students to share teaching strategies, a faculty/staff community for learning about AI (P63).
units.anchor: Open to all University of Minnesota System Staff, Faculty and Students
units.fit_note: Open to students as well as staff and faculty.

units.why: The Faculty Fellows program aims "to foster a multidisciplinary learning community that uses generative AI in teaching practice", a faculty learning community (P63).
units.anchor: foster a multidisciplinary learning community that uses generative AI in teaching practice

documents.title: Avoiding Scholastic Dishonesty
documents.summary: A short Office for Community Standards page of tips for avoiding scholastic dishonesty. Its only AI content is a pointer to the AI FAQ; the other tips (read the syllabus, ask the instructor) are general and not about AI.
documents.stance_why: The page mentions AI once, telling students to "Review frequently asked questions about using generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools in your classes", and sets no stance, so it delegates to the FAQ and the syllabus.

units.why: Among tips to avoid dishonesty, students are told to "Review frequently asked questions about using generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools", i.e. learn the AI rules that apply to them (P78).

notes: Coded 5 included university-layer documents; no school, computing or course documents were collected. The Community Standards page has only one AI mention; its generic tips (read the syllabus, ask the instructor, plan ahead, use tutoring) were not coded because they do not mention AI. Template placeholders in the provost page were coded as the policy they would express; a repeated plagiarism-detection, consequences and reporting line in the permitted template was coded once from the prohibited template.
